content.comment_body: Hello! With experience in various PLC brands, primarily A-B, I'm currently exploring [product_name] for the first time and finding it a bit tricky to navigate [company_name]'s manuals and support resources. I understand that [product_name] focuses more on configuration rather than traditional programming, so I'm curious how it compares to more complex PLCs. Is direct data access possible, similar to using tags in other controllers like S7 or A-B Logix? Additionally, is it possible to access individual bits within different data types? Is there a straightforward explanation of the available data types in [product_name] Settings, especially the meaning of options like X, NQ, NA, M, etc.? Thanks!

Since you haven't specified your exact [product_name] model, I'll assume it's the latest version. Communication with other devices is possible via Ethernet TCP/IP using certain protocols. Similar options are available with other controllers. In general, you're asking for a brief summary of the documentation and online help, which can take a long time to become familiar with, especially as new features get added over time. [product_name] supports programming in FBD or LAD, but LAD may have limitations. The system primarily works with 16-bit integers and bit processing. Manuals and online help detail the intended use of each block. Overall, there are blocks for processing bits, analog values, and some that combine both. I recommend checking the official [company_name] support sites and libraries for practical examples, functions for analog value processing, communication, and further tips via videos and web-based training.

Thank you for the quick response. You're right—I neglected to mention the version, but it is [version_no]. I've looked at several of the reference links you shared but will review them again. My main goal is to understand tag naming and data handling in [product_name]. I am struggling to find adequate documentation specifically about data types, which makes me wonder if [product_name] has any apart from what individual blocks define. Your point about the system being 16-bit is helpful. To explain further, with other platforms, I can declare a tag and assign it a data type, like a DINT, INT, or BOOL, and work with arrays and individual bits within those tags. For example, accessing LEVEL.3 for a fourth bit or LEVEL[2].4 in an array. I've attached a dialogue showing where I/O names are defined and would appreciate a simple guide explaining options like I, Q, X, NA, NAQ, AM, etc. I find it surprising that context-sensitive help doesn't summarize this clearly. For context, I am trying to record a series of analog values for later analysis, while also needing to monitor and control processes in real time. It may turn out that I have to adapt my approach to fit [product_name]'s limitations—it's a learning process!

[product_name] does not provide a tag table like those found in more advanced controllers where you can define data types. The I/O names table is more similar to an assignment list from legacy systems. These names appear in diagrams above the blocks. Some of the meanings: X is an open connector for ending a block with an unlinked digital output, M is for digital flags, AM for analog flags, NI for digital network inputs, NQ for digital network outputs, NAI for analog network inputs, and NAQ for analog network outputs.

analysis.insight_summary: Users who are used to more advanced PLCs are encountering difficulties understanding how data types and variables are organized in [product_name]. The way data is referenced and documented differs notably from larger platforms, resulting in confusion and unmet expectations. Primary concerns include the lack of a clear tag table, uncertainty around data types, and scattered resources explaining symbol functions and variable management.
analysis.user_expectations: Users are looking for accessible documentation that clearly explains the data types, tag naming conventions, and data management in [product_name], similar to the thorough references available for advanced platforms. They expect a centralized, user-friendly resource that helps them understand variable referencing and bit access in the current version.
